title: Sixty contracts in one prompt
scenario: A legal team wants to find every early-cancellation clause in 60 supplier contracts. The contracts total about 410,000 tokens, so they fit in Claude Opus 5.5's 1M-token window. The team sends them in one prompt, but the model finds far fewer clauses than a human review did. You review the prompt layout and the result (exhibit).
exhibit:
PROMPT LAYOUT (Claude Opus 5.5)
1  instructions and question          ~300 tokens
   List every clause that allows early cancellation,
   with the contract name and clause number.
2  all 60 contracts as one JSON array  ~410,000 tokens
   [{"id": 1, "text": "..."}, {"id": 2, "text": "..."}, ...]

RESULT
  model found:          9 clauses
  human review found:  23 clauses

questions.prompt: Following the Claude docs, what is the first layout change?

options.text: Put the 60 contracts first and the question at the end.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say to place long documents above the query, and that queries at the end can improve quality by up to 30 percent in tests.

options.text: Repeat the question before every contract in the array.
options.explanation: That adds 60 copies of the question to an already long prompt. The docs' advice is one query, at the end.

options.text: Keep the question first, but make it longer and more detailed.
options.explanation: A detailed question helps, but the Claude docs' point here is position: long documents on top, the query below them.

options.text: Move the question into a second request sent after the contracts.
options.explanation: The question must be in the same request as the contracts. Within it, the docs put the query after the documents.

questions.prompt: How should each contract be packaged inside the prompt?

options.text: Keep the `[{id, text}]` JSON array, but strip the spaces to save tokens.
options.explanation: Fewer spaces do not fix the structure. OpenAI's GPT-4.1 long-context tests found JSON performed particularly poorly; the Claude docs recommend XML document tags instead.

options.text: Join all contracts into one block of plain text with no breaks.
options.explanation: Then the model cannot tell where one contract ends, so it cannot name the contract for each clause.

options.text: Wrap each in `<document>` tags with a `<source>` subtag.
options.explanation: Right. That is the structure the Claude docs recommend for many documents, and it gives the model the contract name to cite. The text goes in a `<document_content>` subtag.

options.text: Turn each contract into a summary table before sending it.
options.explanation: A summary can drop the exact clause the team needs. The task needs the full text, clearly framed.

questions.prompt: Another team runs the same task on GPT-4.1. Where does OpenAI's GPT-4.1 guide put the instructions?

options.text: Only at the end, after all of the contracts in the prompt.
options.explanation: That matches Claude and Gemini advice, but the GPT-4.1 guide says that if you place instructions once, above the context works better than below.

options.text: In a JSON field next to each contract.
options.explanation: The guide found JSON performed particularly poorly in long-context tests, and it gives no advice to repeat instructions per item.

options.text: Only at the start, and never repeated.
options.explanation: Above is the better single position, but the guide found that placing them at both ends performed better than only above or below.

options.text: At both the beginning and the end of the contracts.
options.explanation: Right. The GPT-4.1 guide found that instructions at both ends performed better than only above or only below.

questions.prompt: Finding 23 clauses means finding many needles at once. What does the Gemini long-context guide suggest for that kind of task?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window, such as 2 million tokens or more.
options.explanation: The contracts already fit. The Gemini guide's concern is accuracy with many needles, not space.

options.text: Ask narrower questions in separate requests and use caching to cut the cost.
options.explanation: Right. Gemini says accuracy drops with many needles, that high accuracy may take one request per item, and that context caching reduces that cost.

options.text: Raise the output token limit so the model can list more clauses.
options.explanation: The model listed 9 of 23, which is not an output-length problem. It missed clauses in the input.

options.text: Send the same single prompt three times and merge the answers.
options.explanation: Three copies of the same broad question repeat the same weakness. The Gemini guide splits the work into narrower requests.
